answers.screener:custom:predicted:question_67916: I'm interested in Appian because the core problem there is process automation inside real institutional workflows, which is the kind of work I keep coming back to. I built a Playwright-based job-application agent in TypeScript where every application moves through an explicit state machine (DISCOVERED to ELIGIBILITY_CHECK to QUEUED to INSPECT to FILL to READY_TO_SUBMIT to SUBMITTED), with SQLite as the single source of truth because browser automation becomes dangerous when application state can diverge across processes. Every mutating capability sits behind fail-closed flags, and free-text and demographic fields are architecturally prevented from being auto-filled and instead route to human review. That project taught me that the hard part of automation is not what a system can do but where it should stop and hand judgment back to a person, which is exactly the tension a workflow platform has to get right for enterprise customers. I've also built systems where the output has to be trusted by someone downstream, not just be technically correct. At Summer Atlantic Capital I own major parts of an anomaly-detection service, including the event-ingestion pipeline, a versioned FastAPI microservice, and a retrieval-augmented explanation layer, because an alert system that floods analysts creates a second problem rather than solving the first. At Intelehealth I designed an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. The part I would want to work on at Appian is where automation, AI, and human decision points meet inside a workflow that a real organization depends on, and I'd want to own a substantial piece of that system rather than isolated tickets.
